cards.title: Exact recognition of bounded clique-width
cards.formal: For every fixed integer k≥1, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A_k and constants C_k,c_k≥1 such that A_k decides whether cw(G)≤k for every finite simple undirected graph G in at most C_k(N+1)^(c_k) steps, where N is the bit length of G’s adjacency-matrix encoding?
cards.why: Tests whether a major dense-graph width parameter admits efficient exact recognition at every fixed value.

cards.definitions: A k-expression is a finite expression building a labeled graph using labels from {1,…,k}. It can create one isolated vertex with a chosen label; take the disjoint union of two previously constructed labeled graphs; add all edges between the vertices labeled i and those labeled j for distinct i,j; or change every label i to j. Edge insertion leaves existing edges in place without duplicating them. Relabeling changes no edges. The two operands of a disjoint union may both be arbitrary expressions, so this is ordinary clique-width, not linear clique-width. For a nonempty graph G, cw(G) is the least k for which some k-expression produces a graph isomorphic to G after labels are erased. Set cw(∅)=0. The input contains n≥0 and the n×n symmetric zero-diagonal 0/1 adjacency matrix for the graph on {1,…,n}. It contains no construction expression or promise about its width. A_k outputs YES exactly when cw(G)≤k and NO otherwise, always halting with the stated worst-case bit bound. The quantifier order is ∀k ∃A_k,C_k,c_k ∀G: k is fixed for each machine, and the polynomial exponent may depend on it. Each A_k is a single finite program with no advice depending on graph size; the statement imposes no effective map from k to its program and no uniform exponent.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time exact recognition for every fixed threshold k in the model stated, or prove that for at least one fixed k the language {G:cw(G)≤k} has no deterministic polynomial-time decider. An expression with more than k labels does not establish a YES answer; failure of one construction does not establish NO. Variable-k NP-hardness, or fixed-k hardness under an unproved assumption, does not alone unconditionally refute this proposition.

context_blocks.title: A width that permits dense graphs
context_blocks.text: Clique-width counts reusable labels in a construction, not the size of a largest clique. Every nonempty edgeless graph has width 1. Complete graphs with at least two vertices have width 2, regardless of their size. Thus even very dense graphs can have small clique-width; the parameter captures how uniformly groups of vertices can be assembled.

context_blocks.title: Fixed thresholds versus the general optimization problem
context_blocks.text: Fellows and coauthors prove NP-completeness when both G and k are input. The present statement allows a different polynomial bound for each fixed k. For example, a hypothetical bound N^(k+2) would be polynomial for each such threshold, while not giving a polynomial bound when k grows with N. The source lists fixed-threshold recognition separately from the stronger FPT question, which asks for one algorithm with runtime f(k)N^c and c independent of k.

context_blocks.title: Small thresholds are understood
context_blocks.text: Polynomial-time recognition is known through k=3, with the full three-label algorithm published by Corneil and coauthors in 2012. The cited sources retain k=4 as the first unresolved threshold. A solution only for four labels would still leave the card’s quantification over every fixed k.

context_blocks.title: Approximate or supplied decompositions serve a different purpose
context_blocks.text: A procedure that returns an expression with f(k)>k labels for graphs of width at most k can enable other graph algorithms, yet leave the exact threshold undecided. Likewise, the July 2026 feedback-vertex-set result assumes a k-expression is already supplied. These results explain the usefulness of clique-width without providing the recognizer requested here.

sentences: Clique-width measures how many reusable vertex labels are needed to build a graph with four specified operations.
Even a complete graph of arbitrary size needs only two labels.
The question asks whether graphs of width at most k can be recognized in polynomial time for every fixed k.
The polynomial exponent may depend on k, so known NP-completeness when k is input does not settle it.
Small thresholds are understood, while approximate or supplied decompositions do not give exact recognition at every threshold.

cards.context:
Clique-width counts reusable labels in a construction, not the size of a largest clique. Every nonempty edgeless graph has width 1. Complete graphs with at least two vertices have width 2, regardless of their size. Thus even very dense graphs can have small clique-width; the parameter captures how uniformly groups of vertices can be assembled.

Fellows and coauthors prove NP-completeness when both G and k are input. The present statement allows a different polynomial bound for each fixed k. For example, a hypothetical bound N^(k+2) would be polynomial for each such threshold, while not giving a polynomial bound when k grows with N. The source lists fixed-threshold recognition separately from the stronger FPT question, which asks for one algorithm with runtime f(k)N^c and c independent of k.

Polynomial-time recognition is known through k=3, with the full three-label algorithm published by Corneil and coauthors in 2012. The cited sources retain k=4 as the first unresolved threshold. A solution only for four labels would still leave the card’s quantification over every fixed k.

A procedure that returns an expression with f(k)>k labels for graphs of width at most k can enable other graph algorithms, yet leave the exact threshold undecided. Likewise, the July 2026 feedback-vertex-set result assumes a k-expression is already supplied. These results explain the usefulness of clique-width without providing the recognizer requested here.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
